$comment: Serena hooks (https://github.com/oraios/serena). Recommended by Serena's own docs, which report
that Claude Code's built-in tool descriptions take ~16k tokens and bias Opus strongly toward
internal tools -- strongly enough that the agent will often not reach for Serena at all, or will
forget to during a long session (agent drift).
Serena calls hooks an ALPHA feature. Each is opt-in; delete any you do not want.
remind       nudges the agent toward Serena's symbolic tools after several consecutive
grep/read_file calls with no Serena tool in between.
activate     asks the agent to activate the project and read Serena's instructions at
session start.
auto-approve auto-approves Serena tool calls ONLY when Claude Code is already in a permissive
permission mode (acceptEdits or auto), so an existing blanket approval also covers
Serena's destructive tools (replace_symbol_body, rename_symbol) instead of
prompting per call. It grants nothing the chosen mode does not already grant.
cleanup      discards hook session state when the session ends.
These require the `serena-hooks` executable on PATH (installed with serena-agent). If Serena is
not installed the hooks fail harmlessly, but see README.md for the one-time setup.
scripts/guard.py enforces traps CLAUDE.md already documents, because prose that has to be read
to be obeyed is obeyed inconsistently. Three severities, and the split is the design:
deny   RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP=1 on cargo (hashed into the build fingerprint, so it recompiles the
workspace under a flag that admits nightly features silently), and `git commit` while
`cargo fmt --check` fails. Both are SILENTLY wrong -- they produce an answer that is
not about what you think. Escape with SKIP_JDWP_AGENT_GUARD=1 in the command.
ask    `git push`. Not unsafe, but this repo's release flow commits and tags while
deliberately NOT pushing, so a push is the user's call rather than the agent's.
warn   a soak loop against the working tree, a hardcoded --shard N/M, a --test-threads
override, and unbounded full-workspace cargo output. Emitted as additionalContext, so
the model reads it and the command still runs -- `probably` is doing real work in each
of these and a block would strand a legitimate run.
The rules live in scripts/guard.py and NOT in .claude/ (LINT-7, #167). Five of the seven used to
hold for exactly one host, so a plain shell, another agent or a script in CI got none of them and
the tree could not check itself. .claude/hooks/pre-bash-guard.py is now an adapter that calls
check() and renders the JSON above; it holds no policy. Any host can ask the same question:
scripts/guard.py check 'RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP=1 cargo test'    # prints the verdict; exits 20
Nothing calls it automatically outside Claude Code, and that is worth knowing rather than
assuming: elsewhere this is a command you run, not a guard that runs.
The guard is tested: `bash scripts/guard.test.sh` runs 32 cases -- 28 against the checker, of
which 17 are must-NOT-fire (a heredoc mentioning RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP, an echo containing `git push`,
a grep for --shard in the docs), plus 4 through the adapter, one per verdict shape, because each
maps to a different key and a `warn` rendered as a decision would start blocking commands that
are meant to proceed. THREE real tokenizer bugs have been found by that matrix or in the wild,
never by reading: `40);` as one token, `);` re-grouped, and heredoc BODIES lexed as commands --
the last one fired the soak-loop rule on a `git commit` whose message quoted a test run. THAT
COUNT IS ASSERTED by mcp-server/tests/docs_claims.rs, so this comment cannot quietly go stale.
statusline.py surfaces this repo's invisible states: branch (amber on main), workspace version,
dirty count, unpushed commits, and -- the one that earns its slot -- an annotated tag on HEAD
that the remote does not have, which is exactly what `scripts/release.sh` leaves behind by
design.
